title: Rose Philippine Duchesne (18 November)
hookLine: a French sister who went west in America; the Potawatomi called her the woman who always prays

lines: AN OLD WOMAN ON THE PRAIRIE.
cards: An old woman kneels in a small mission chapel on the Kansas prairie. She has come a long way to be here, and she can't speak the language of the people she came to serve. So she does the one thing left to her.
She prays, for hours, in the chapel. The Potawatomi people of the mission watch her, and they give her a name. In English it's usually given as the woman who prays always.
She couldn't teach in words, and she taught anyway.

teach.h: A FRENCH NUN WITH A FIXED DREAM.
teach.b: Rose Philippine Duchesne was born in France, in Grenoble, to a well-off family.

She became a nun young, lived through the upheaval of the French Revolution when convents were shut, and afterward joined a new order, the Society of the Sacred Heart, founded by Madeleine Sophie Barat to educate girls.
From early on Philippine had a fixed dream: to go to America and teach the native peoples there.
For years she asked; for years she was told to wait. At last she crossed the ocean with a few sisters to the Mississippi valley and set up a school in Saint Charles, in Missouri.
It was hard: cold, poverty, illness, and a new language she never mastered. She ran schools and convents for years, and much of it felt to her like failure.

teach.h: OLD AND FRAIL, TO SUGAR CREEK.
teach.b: Then, when she was old and frail, the Jesuits asked for sisters at their mission among the Potawatomi at Sugar Creek in Kansas. Others thought she was too weak to go.

A priest said, in effect, that she must come: even if she could do little work, she would pray, and that would draw down blessings. So she went, and that's how she spent her time there, praying in the chapel.
The story goes that curious children would put bits of paper on the hem of her habit while she knelt, and come back hours later to find them still there.
It's Paul's line, taken at its word: "Pray without ceasing." Her dream had been to teach. What she gave them was a picture of prayer that they put into a name.

how: Catholics in the United States keep the memorial of Saint Rose Philippine Duchesne on 18 November, and schools of the Society of the Sacred Heart mark her feast.

games.q: you're old and frail, and a mission opens far west among people whose language you can't learn. what do you do?
o: stay home; you'd be no use.
games.why: Philippine went, and spent her days praying in the chapel; the Potawatomi named her for it.

practice: Kneel or sit as Philippine did, and stay still, as if a scrap of paper were resting on your sleeve. Think of the places your day already pauses, waking, a meal, a door you walk through, and choose one more pause to add.
If you pray, pray now with a line you already know, or in silence; if you don't, let this pause be a breath and a moment of attention.

wordCard.voice: Philippine. A French sister of the Society of the Sacred Heart who taught in Missouri and prayed among the Potawatomi in Kansas.

carryVoice: Your line: she who always prays. Where her words failed, her prayer still spoke. Until tomorrow.
